summary.text: By counting pairs divisible by each power of a prime and using the corresponding factorial valuation formula, the proof expresses the valuation as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor^2-\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r\le N}r\lfloor N/(rq^i)\rfloor\), with divisibility justified by \(\sum_r r\lfloor M/r\rfloor\le M^2\). For \(N=np+k\) with \(k<p\), division by every positive power of \(p\) depends only on \(\lfloor N/p\rfloor=n\), and the extra terms indexed by \(np<r\le np+k\) vanish, so both sums equal those for \(N=np\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
G(N)=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{r=1}^{N}\gcd(j,r),
\qquad
D(N)=\prod_{r=1}^{N}\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nr\right\rfloor !\right)^r.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
a(N)=\frac{G(N)}{D(N)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and derive a formula for its prime-adic valuation. We will then show directly from that formula that the valuation is constant as claimed.

For a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of \(x\). Fix an integer \(B\) such that
\[
N<q^B.
\]
We claim that
\[
 v_q(G(N))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for positive \(j,r\),
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,r))=\min(v_q(j),v_q(r)).
\]
Since \(j,r\le N<q^B\), both \(v_q(j)\) and \(v_q(r)\) are less than \(B\). Hence
\[
\min(v_q(j),v_q(r))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j\,\text{ and }\,q^i\mid r},
\]
because the summand is one precisely for the integers \(i\) with
\(1\le i\le \min(v_q(j),v_q(r))\). Taking valuations in the product defining \(G(N)\), and then interchanging the finite sums, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(G(N))
&=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N}v_q(\gcd(j,r))\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}\right)
  \left(\sum_{r=1}^{N}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
There are exactly \(\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) between \(1\) and \(N\), proving (1).

Next we claim that
\[
 v_q(D(N))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\sum_{r=1}^{N}
 r\left\lfloor\frac{N}{r q^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]
To see this, recall Legendre's formula
\[
v_q(m!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
For completeness, this follows by writing
\(v_q(m!)=\sum_{t=1}^m v_q(t)\), expressing \(v_q(t)\) as the number of positive \(i\) for which \(q^i\mid t\), and interchanging the two sums. For each \(i\), the number of multiples of \(q^i\) in \(1,\ldots,m\) is \(\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\).

In our application, \(m=\lfloor N/r\rfloor\le N<q^B\), so all terms with \(i\ge B\) vanish. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(N))
&=\sum_{r=1}^{N}r\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nr\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{r=1}^{N}r\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Successive integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{r q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Interchanging the finite sums proves (2).

We also need to know that \(D(N)\) really divides \(G(N)\). For each \(i\), put
\[
M=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Using successive integer division once more,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N}{r q^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{M}{r}\right\rfloor.
\]
We now establish the elementary estimate
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{N}r\left\lfloor\frac Mr\right\rfloor\le M^2. \tag{3}
\]
There are two cases for each index \(r\). If \(r\le M\), then
\[
r\left\lfloor\frac Mr\right\rfloor\le M.
\]
If \(r>M\), then \(\lfloor M/r\rfloor=0\), so the summand is zero. Thus only indices \(r\le M\) can contribute, there are at most \(M\) such indices, and each contributes at most \(M\). This proves (3).

Applying (3) for every \(i=1,\ldots,B-1\) and comparing (1) and (2), we obtain
\[
v_q(D(N))\le v_q(G(N)) \tag{4}
\]
for every prime \(q\). Both \(G(N)\) and \(D(N)\) are nonzero: every gcd in \(G(N)\) is positive, and every factorial in \(D(N)\) is positive. By unique prime factorization, (4) for every prime implies
\[
D(N)\mid G(N).
\]
Consequently \(a(N)=G(N)/D(N)\) is an integer, and subtraction of prime exponents gives
\[
\boxed{
 v_q(a(N))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2
 -\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\sum_{r=1}^{N}
 r\left\lfloor\frac{N}{r q^i}\right\rfloor
} \tag{5}
\]
whenever \(N<q^B\). The subtraction in (5) is ordinary nonnegative integer subtraction because of (4).

We now apply (5) to the prime \(p\) occurring in the conjecture. Let \(n\ge1\), let \(p\) be prime, and let
\[
0\le k<p.
\]
Set
\[
N_0=np,\qquad N_1=np+k.
\]
Because \(k<p\), division by \(p\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{p}\right\rfloor=n,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{p}\right\rfloor=n. \tag{6}
\]
We compare separately the two sums in (5).

First, for every \(i\ge1\), successive division by \(p\) and then by \(p^{i-1}\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}{p^{i-1}}
\right\rfloor.
\]
Using (6), we therefore have
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{7}
\]
It follows term by term from (7) that the first, numerator-derived sum in (5) has the same value for \(N_0\) and \(N_1\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2. \tag{8}
\]

Now consider the denominator-derived sum. For every \(i\ge1\) and every positive \(r\), factor
\[
r p^i=p\bigl(rp^{i-1}\bigr).
\]
Successive integer division, followed by (6), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{r p^i}\right\rfloor
&=\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor N_1/p\rfloor}{r p^{i-1}}
 \right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{n}{r p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{r p^i}\right\rfloor
&=\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor N_0/p\rfloor}{r p^{i-1}}
 \right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{n}{r p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor. \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the summand, after division by the initial factor \(p\), is the same function of \(r\) for \(N_0\) and \(N_1\). The only apparent difference is that the sum for \(N_1\) ranges up to \(np+k\), while the sum for \(N_0\) ranges only up to \(np\).

We show that every extra summand is zero. Suppose
\[
np<r\le np+k.
\]
Since \(p>0\), we have \(n\le np<r\), and hence \(r>n\). Also \(p^{i-1}\ge1\), so
\[
r p^{i-1}\ge r>n.
\]
It follows that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{r p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
By (9), the summands indexed by all such extra \(r\) vanish. Therefore, for each \(i\ge1\),
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{N_1}r\left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{r p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\sum_{r=1}^{N_0}r\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{r p^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{10}
\]
Summing (10) over \(i=1,\ldots,B-1\) shows that the second sum in (5) is also identical for \(N_0\) and \(N_1\).

It remains only to choose one truncation bound \(B\) for which (5) applies to both numbers. Take
\[
B=N_1+1=np+k+1.
\]
A prime satisfies \(p\ge2\), and for every nonnegative integer \(m\),
\[
m<p^{m+1}.
\]
For instance, \(p^{m+1}\ge2^{m+1}>m\), with the last inequality following immediately by induction. Applying this with \(m=N_1\) gives
\[
N_1<p^B.
\]
Since \(N_0\le N_1\), we also have \(N_0<p^B\). Thus formula (5) is valid for both \(N_0\) and \(N_1\) with this common value of \(B\).

Finally, (8) says their numerator-derived valuation sums agree, and (10) says their denominator-derived valuation sums agree. Subtracting the equal quantities in (5) gives
\[
v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+k)).
\]
This holds for every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
=\cdots=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as required.
